issues.legal_issue: A beneficiary’s subsidy under an investment incentive scheme is limited to the scheme’s ordinary cap when the enhanced cement-industry incentive has been withdrawn and no competent authority approved a higher subsidy under the scheme’s general enhancement mechanism.
material_facts: The scheme ordinarily capped the subsidy at 50% of the relevant tax, while a separate cement-industry provision permitting a higher subsidy had been deleted before the eligibility application was decided.
The earlier board resolution stated that the recently announced cement package and the scheme would apply, but did not approve a higher subsidy under the scheme’s general enhancement mechanism.
The screening committee later treated the board resolution as approval for a 75% subsidy and issued entitlement certificates on that basis.
The company claimed eligibility under the deleted cement-specific provision; the record showed no recommendation and approval for a customized incentive package.
issues.conclusion: The company was entitled to subsidy only up to 50% of the payable and deposited tax, not 75%; the certificates granting the higher subsidy were erroneous and the excess was recoverable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Clauses 6, 6A and 7(i)(a)–(b) of the Rajasthan Investment Promotion Scheme-2003, the screening committee determined eligibility, while an increase above the ordinary cap required the prescribed approval. The board’s general direction to apply the cement package and the scheme did not itself approve a higher subsidy under the general enhancement proviso or grant a customized package. The deleted cement-specific provisions could not confer an entitlement after their deletion. Incentive and exemption provisions are strictly construed, and an ambiguity does not benefit the claimant: Commissioner of Customs (Import), Mumbai v. Dilip Kumar & Co. and Ramnath & Co. v. Commissioner of Income Tax. The Court also referred to J.K. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P. in considering the relationship between specific and general provisions.

rule.if: investment_subsidy_claim and ordinary_scheme_cap_applies and cement_specific_incentive_withdrawn_before_eligibility_decision and no_competent_approval_for_higher_subsidy

predicates.investment_subsidy_claim: An industrial unit sought a subsidy under an investment incentive scheme.
predicates.ordinary_scheme_cap_applies: The applicable scheme set an ordinary maximum for the subsidy.
predicates.cement_specific_incentive_withdrawn_befo: The scheme’s separate enhanced incentive for cement units had been withdrawn before the unit’s eligibility was decided.
predicates.no_competent_approval_for_higher_subsidy: No authority prescribed to approve a higher subsidy or customized package had approved one for the unit.

issues.definition: When a unit seeks an investment subsidy, the ordinary scheme cap applies if that cap governs, the sector-specific enhancement has been withdrawn, and no competent authority approved a higher subsidy.

issues.legal_issue: A contemporaneous administrative interpretation does not control when the interpretation is clearly erroneous.
material_facts: The screening committee relied on the board’s earlier resolution to grant a higher subsidy, although the resolution did not approve that subsidy.
The committee’s interpretation was inconsistent with the scheme’s terms and with the withdrawal of the cement-specific incentive before the eligibility decision.
The company relied on the committee’s interpretation as a contemporaneous construction of the scheme.
issues.conclusion: The doctrine of contemporanea expositio did not apply to make the screening committee’s erroneous interpretation binding or to benefit the company.
issues.legal_principle: Contemporanea expositio may guide construction by reference to an exposition given by competent contemporary authority, and an administrative construction may carry persuasive weight, but it is not binding and may be rejected when clearly wrong. The Court relied on Desh Bandhu Gupta v. Delhi Stock Exchange Association Ltd. and the principles discussed in Maxwell and Crawford on Statutory Construction; it also noted that the doctrine is not invariably applicable and distinguished Spentex Industries Ltd. v. C.C.E., where the same government had framed the rules and issued the relevant notifications. An erroneous administrative understanding is not immune from judicial scrutiny.

predicates.interpretation_dispute_in_scheme_proceed: A dispute concerns the interpretation of an incentive scheme in a proceeding about benefits under that scheme.
predicates.contemporaneous_administrative_interpret: An administrative authority applied an interpretation while administering the scheme at the relevant time.
predicates.interpretation_clearly_erroneous: The authority’s interpretation conflicts with the scheme’s terms or the facts governing the claimed benefit.

issues.definition: A contemporaneous administrative interpretation is not controlling when it was given in a scheme-benefit dispute and is clearly erroneous.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot compel the State to honour an unauthorized benefit where no specific representation of that benefit was made.
material_facts: The board directed that the recently announced cement package and the scheme would apply, but did not direct that the company receive a 75% subsidy.
The later memorandum of understanding promised incentives permissible under the scheme and the prevalent policy, not a fixed higher subsidy.
The company invested in the project, but no application seeking an increase under the general enhancement mechanism was placed before the competent board while it existed.
The higher subsidy was granted later through screening committee decisions that were unauthorized and inconsistent with the applicable scheme.
issues.conclusion: Promissory estoppel did not prevent the State from withdrawing the excess subsidy or exercising its revisional power.
issues.legal_principle: Promissory estoppel requires a representation that induced a change of position and cannot enforce a promise contrary to law or beyond the authority of the person making it. The Court relied on Dr. Ashok Kumar Maheshwari v. State of U.P., which referred to Kasinka Trading v. Union of India and Shabi Construction Co. v. City & Industrial Development Corporation. A promise limited to benefits permissible under the scheme does not represent that an unauthorized higher benefit will be given; nor does estoppel defeat a revisional power reserved under the scheme.

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim: A beneficiary claims that the State is prevented from withdrawing a benefit because the beneficiary relied on a governmental promise.
predicates.no_specific_representation_of_higher_ben: The State made no specific representation that the beneficiary would receive the higher benefit claimed.
predicates.higher_benefit_granted_without_authority: The higher benefit was granted by an authority acting beyond the benefit permitted by the applicable scheme.

issues.definition: Promissory estoppel does not bar recovery when the State made no specific representation of the higher benefit and the benefit was granted without authority.

issues.legal_issue: The State may revise an erroneous screening committee decision prejudicial to public revenue within the scheme’s prescribed period, even after the beneficiary has received the benefit.
material_facts: The screening committee granted a subsidy beyond the applicable ordinary cap by misconstruing the board’s resolution and the scheme.
The additional subsidy caused the State to pay more than the scheme permitted, prejudicing public revenue.
The State initiated revision within five years after the benefits had been fully availed.
The beneficiary had already received the excess subsidy before the revision was completed.
issues.conclusion: The State validly exercised its revisional power and could recover the excess subsidy despite the beneficiary having already availed the benefit.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 13 of the Rajasthan Investment Promotion Scheme-2003 authorized the State Government to revise a screening committee order that was both erroneous and prejudicial to State revenue, subject to the time limit in Clause 13(b). The Court held that the screening committee’s decision was not a possible view and that the two requirements were met. It considered Malabar Industrial Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Kerala State, which explains that revenue loss alone is insufficient where an authority has adopted a permissible view, but supports revision where the order is erroneous and unsustainable. The scheme expressly allowed revision within five years after the benefits were fully availed, so prior receipt of the benefit did not prevent recovery.

rule.if: scheme_benefit_revision_proceeding and screening_decision_erroneous and decision_prejudices_public_revenue and revision_started_within_permitted_window

predicates.scheme_benefit_revision_proceeding: The matter is a revision of a screening committee decision granting benefits under an incentive scheme.
predicates.screening_decision_erroneous: The screening committee granted a benefit by misconstruing the governing scheme or the relevant decision on which it relied.
predicates.decision_prejudices_public_revenue: The decision requires public funds to be paid beyond the benefit allowed by the scheme.
predicates.revision_started_within_permitted_window: The State began revision within the period allowed after the beneficiary had fully availed the scheme benefits.

issues.definition: An erroneous screening decision that prejudices public revenue may be revised within the permitted window, and excess benefits may be recovered even after receipt.

issues.legal_issue: The beneficiary is not liable for the scheme’s higher interest rate absent breach or misrepresentation, but remains liable for the lower interest rate it undertook to pay on excess benefits.
material_facts: The excess subsidy resulted from erroneous screening committee decisions, not from a breach of the scheme’s conditions or a misrepresentation by the company.
The scheme provided for 18% interest where a condition was breached, but the State did not allege such a breach as the basis for recovering the excess subsidy.
In its application, the company undertook to repay excess benefits with interest at 12% per annum.
The company had obtained a monetary benefit by receiving subsidy above its entitlement.
issues.conclusion: The State could recover the excess subsidy with interest at 12% per annum from the date the excess subsidy was availed until payment or recovery, but not at 18% per annum.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 10 of the Rajasthan Investment Promotion Scheme-2003 imposed interest at 18% where recovery followed a breach of the scheme’s conditions. Because no breach or misrepresentation caused the excess payment, Clause 10 did not authorize that rate. The undertaking in the application to repay excess benefits with 12% interest was a binding term between the parties, and the beneficiary remained liable at that agreed rate. The Court distinguished India Carbon Ltd. v. State of Assam, J.K. Synthetics Ltd. v. C.T.O. and Maruti Wire Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. Sales Tax Officer, which concerned interest under particular taxing statutes and did not eliminate liability under the undertaking.

predicates.excess_scheme_subsidy_repayment_dispute: The State seeks repayment of subsidy paid beyond the beneficiary’s entitlement under a scheme.
predicates.no_breach_or_misrepresentation_caused_ex: The excess payment resulted from an authority’s error rather than the beneficiary’s breach of conditions or misrepresentation.
predicates.beneficiary_undertook_lower_interest_on_: The beneficiary agreed to repay excess benefits with interest at a specified rate lower than the scheme’s breach-related rate.

issues.definition: When excess subsidy resulted from official error without beneficiary breach or misrepresentation, and the beneficiary undertook to repay it with interest, recovery is subject to the rate in that undertaking.
